solution.concept_anchor: MGNREGA social audit statutory mandate — Section 17
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know that SAUs are involved in MGNREGA social audits may assume the SAU (not the Gram Sabha) is the primary body mandated to conduct audits, reversing the principal-agent relationship.
elimination_logic: Identify what the scenario describes: a village-level meeting of all voters that scrutinises wage payment records, job card entries, and work completion certificates for a public employment scheme.
This is clearly a social audit under MGNREGA — the scheme, the records, and the village-level meeting format all point to MGNREGA Section 17.
Eliminate (b): SAUs facilitate but are not the primary body mandated to conduct social audits — Gram Sabha is the mandated body under Section 17.
Eliminate (c): Gram Panchayat is the implementing body being audited — it cannot be the auditing body simultaneously; this would defeat the purpose of accountability.
Eliminate (d): CAG audit is a national-level financial audit — not a village-level social audit of specific work records.
Confirm (a): Gram Sabha conducting social audit under Section 17 of MGNREGA — the scenario precisely describes this statutory function.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes the Social Audit Unit for the Gram Sabha. Students who know SAUs are involved in MGNREGA social audits may believe the SAU is the primary auditing body. In reality, SAUs are support/facilitation bodies — the STATUTORY mandate for social audit under Section 17 of MGNREGA is placed on the Gram Sabha itself. SAUs provide technical support and independence to the Gram Sabha's audit process, but the Gram Sabha is the legally mandated auditing body.
solution.final_explanation:
MGNREGA's social audit mechanism is the most significant statutory accountability function of the Gram Sabha in Indian law.

Scenario analysis: The scenario describes a village meeting of all registered voters scrutinising job cards, muster rolls, and work completion certificates for a public employment scheme. This matches the social audit process under Section 17 of MGNREGA — where Gram Sabha is statutorily mandated to conduct regular audits of all MGNREGA works in its jurisdiction.

• Option (a) — Correct: Section 17 of MGNREGA places a statutory obligation on Gram Sabha to conduct social audits of all works undertaken under the scheme — the scenario exactly describes this function.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: SAUs are independent state-level bodies that facilitate the social audit process; they are not the primary body mandated by Section 17 — that is the Gram Sabha.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Gram Panchayat is the implementing body of MGNREGA works and is the subject of the social audit — it cannot simultaneously be the auditing body.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CAG audits are financial/compliance audits conducted at a macro level — not village-level social audits of specific works.

Value Addition:
• Social audit under MGNREGA is the ONLY instance where Gram Sabha has a statutory (not advisory) audit mandate.
• Programme Officers under MGNREGA rules must act on social audit findings within 30 days.
• The Rajasthan MKSS model of Jan Sunwai was the inspiration for Section 17's social audit provision.

elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: states where Part IX (including constitutional Gram Sabha) does NOT apply or is significantly limited due to constitutional exemptions.
Option (a) Nagaland: Exempted from Part IX under Article 371A — Gram Sabha as a constitutional institution is absent.
Option (b) Odisha: Part IX DOES apply to Odisha — it is one of the 10 PESA states. Gram Sabha functions under both Part IX and PESA in Odisha. This is the odd one out.
Option (c) Manipur: Hill areas of Manipur have limited Panchayati Raj application — valley areas have Part IX application, but the tribal hill districts are exempted.
Option (d) Mizoram: Covered by Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils) — Part IX does not apply.
Odisha is the only state among these four where constitutional Gram Sabha under Part IX applies fully — it is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic swap trap places Odisha among states known for limited or absent Panchayati Raj application. Students who associate Odisha with tribal issues (given its significant tribal population and Niyamgiri case prominence) may incorrectly classify it as a state with limited Part IX application. In reality, Odisha is a regular Part IX state and one of the 10 PESA states — its tribal governance is through the Gram Sabha itself (under PESA), not through Autonomous District Councils.
solution.final_explanation:
Part IX's constitutional Gram Sabha framework does not apply uniformly across all Indian states due to explicit constitutional exemptions.

• Option (a) Nagaland — Part IX does not apply: Article 371A gives Nagaland special provisions protecting its customary laws; Part IX (Panchayati Raj including constitutional Gram Sabha) does not apply.
• Option (b) Odisha — the odd one out: Odisha is a regular Part IX state with full Panchayati Raj application. Moreover, it is one of the 10 PESA states — its tribal-area Gram Sabhas have enhanced powers. The constitutional Gram Sabha functions normally here.
• Option (c) Manipur — partial application: Manipur's tribal hill areas are exempted from Part IX under Article 371C and related provisions; valley areas have Panchayati Raj but hill tribal districts function differently.
• Option (d) Mizoram — Part IX does not apply: Mizoram is a Sixth Schedule state with Autonomous District Councils — Part IX provisions, including the constitutional Gram Sabha, are not operative there.

Value Addition:
• The four Sixth Schedule states are Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram — all northeastern.
• Dorbar Shnong (Meghalaya) and similar traditional institutions function like Gram Sabhas but are not constitutional bodies.
• PESA's 10 states are all non-northeastern — this is a critical geographic distinction for UPSC.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243G and Eleventh Schedule — 'may' not 'shall', 29 subjects

statement_analysis.statement: Article 243G uses the word 'shall' — making it constitutionally mandatory for state legislatures to empower Gram Panchayats to prepare plans for economic development and social justice across all 29 subjects in the Eleventh Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243G uses 'may', not 'shall' — state legislatures have complete discretion to decide whether and to what extent to endow Panchayats with planning functions. The 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects are a reference list, not a mandatory assignment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Eleventh Schedule to the Constitution lists 29 subjects across which Gram Panchayats may be given planning functions — these include agriculture, social forestry, poverty alleviation programmes, and primary health care.
statement_analysis.reason: The Eleventh Schedule does list 29 subjects including agriculture, social forestry, poverty alleviation, and primary health care — these are the subjects across which state legislatures may optionally devolve planning functions to Panchayats.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 243ZD provides for the constitution of District Planning Committees to consolidate plans prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities — Gram Sabha's bottom-up planning inputs feed into this process.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243ZD mandates the constitution of District Planning Committees in every district to consolidate plans prepared by Panchayats (including Gram Panchayats whose plans are informed by Gram Sabha inputs) and Municipalities — creating the link between Gram Sabha deliberations and district-level planning.

statement_analysis.statement: Activity Mapping under the Eleventh Schedule determines which Panchayat tier (village, intermediate, or district) handles which function — and the Gram Sabha has a formal constitutional role in approving this activity mapping for its village.
statement_analysis.reason: Activity Mapping is an administrative exercise conducted by state governments to assign functions across the three tiers of Panchayati Raj. It is not a constitutional process, and Gram Sabha has no formal constitutional role in approving activity mapping — it is a state-level administrative determination.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is a strong distractor because statements 2 and 3 are correct but students who know Activity Mapping involves Panchayats may incorrectly credit Statement 4 as correct, giving them three and selecting option (c) incorrectly for the wrong reason — or they may doubt Statement 1 and choose 'only one'.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 243G uses 'may' — not 'shall'. Describing it as mandatory is factually wrong. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Eleventh Schedule does list 29 subjects including agriculture, social forestry, poverty alleviation, and primary health care. Statement 2 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 243ZD does provide for District Planning Committees — Gram Sabha inputs flow upward through this planning chain. Statement 3 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Activity Mapping is a state government administrative exercise — Gram Sabha has no formal constitutional approval role in it. Statement 4 is Incorrect.
Two statements (2 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's 'shall' substitution for 'may' is the primary trap. Students who associate the 73rd Amendment with mandatory decentralisation frequently mark this as correct. Statement 4 exploits knowledge of Activity Mapping — a term that appears in Panchayati Raj literature — by attributing to the Gram Sabha a constitutional approval role that it does not have. Students who know Activity Mapping is a real concept but are uncertain about its exact legal character may credit Statement 4 without knowing it is a state administrative exercise, not a constitutional process.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243G and the Eleventh Schedule together define the planning dimension of Gram Panchayat — with Gram Sabha as the deliberative input mechanism.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 243G uses 'may' — the devolution of planning functions to Panchayats is discretionary for state legislatures. This is the fundamental constitutional gap in decentralised planning.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects including agriculture, social forestry, fisheries, poverty alleviation, primary health, and education — the reference framework for optional devolution to Panchayats.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 243ZD mandates District Planning Committees to integrate Panchayat and Municipal plans at the district level — Gram Sabha deliberations are the base of this bottom-up planning chain.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Activity Mapping is a state government administrative exercise assigning functions across Panchayat tiers. Gram Sabha has no constitutional role in approving or validating activity mapping — this is an executive/administrative state function.

Value Addition:
• Article 243ZD's District Planning Committees are constitutionally mandated — unlike most other Part IX provisions that use 'may'.
• Of the 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects, few have been fully transferred to Panchayats in most states.
• The 3Fs of devolution — Functions, Funds, and Functionaries — must all be transferred for meaningful decentralisation.

solution.concept_anchor: Gram Sabha resolutions — binding in PESA areas, recommendatory in non-PESA areas

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: In PESA-covered Scheduled Areas, Gram Sabha resolutions on land acquisition and mining have a quasi-binding character — the government must obtain Gram Sabha consent/consultation before proceeding, making simple overriding of such resolutions legally untenable.
statement_analysis.reason: PESA mandates prior consultation with Gram Sabha before land acquisition, displacement, and mining in Scheduled Areas. The Niyamgiri ruling further reinforced that Gram Sabha's determination must be obtained and is not merely advisory — giving resolutions a quasi-binding character in this context.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: In non-PESA areas, a Gram Sabha resolution passed by a majority of members present automatically overrides any conflicting Gram Panchayat decision on the same matter, as the Gram Sabha is constitutionally the superior body.
statement_analysis.reason: In non-PESA areas, Gram Sabha resolutions are generally recommendatory unless state law specifically gives them binding status. A Gram Sabha resolution cannot automatically override a Gram Panchayat's formal executive decision — Gram Sabha's superiority is deliberative/political, not automatically legally superior to specific Gram Panchayat executive decisions in most states.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know that Gram Sabha is constitutionally the 'principal' may assume this translates into automatic legal superiority over Gram Panchayat decisions in all areas, making both statements appear correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: PESA's mandatory consultation and Niyamgiri ruling establish quasi-binding character for Gram Sabha resolutions in Scheduled Areas — factually accurate. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: In non-PESA areas, Gram Sabha resolutions are recommendatory by default — they do NOT automatically override Gram Panchayat executive decisions unless state law explicitly provides otherwise. The phrase 'automatically overrides' makes this claim factually incorrect. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the principal-agent framework between Gram Sabha and Gram Panchayat. Students who have internalised that 'Gram Sabha is the principal, Gram Panchayat is the agent' may logically conclude that Gram Sabha resolutions automatically override Gram Panchayat decisions. This constitutional design principle does not translate into automatic legal override in practice — in non-PESA areas, the binding or overriding effect of Gram Sabha resolutions depends entirely on what state law provides.
solution.final_explanation:
The binding nature of Gram Sabha resolutions varies sharply between PESA and non-PESA areas.

• Statement 1 — Correct: In Fifth Schedule areas covered by PESA, Gram Sabha resolutions on land acquisition, mining, and displacement have a quasi-binding character. Government agencies must obtain Gram Sabha consent before proceeding, and post-Niyamgiri (2013), courts have treated non-compliance with this requirement as legally untenable.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: In non-PESA areas, no constitutional provision makes Gram Sabha resolutions automatically binding on or superior to Gram Panchayat executive decisions. The relationship is deliberative and political — Gram Sabha can question, reject plans, and withhold approval (if state law so provides), but 'automatic override' is not the legal position. Kerala is exceptional in giving Gram Sabha statutory powers to approve or reject Panchayat plans.

Value Addition:
• High Courts can review Gram Sabha resolutions if they violate fundamental rights or state law — Gram Sabha is not above judicial review.
• The distinction between 'accountability to Gram Sabha' (constitutional) and 'legal override by Gram Sabha' (state law dependent) is critical.
• In most states, Gram Panchayat executive decisions can be challenged by Gram Sabha only through state-prescribed grievance or appeal mechanisms, not automatic legal override.

solution.concept_anchor: 73rd Amendment 'may' clause creates asymmetric Gram Sabha empowerment
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume that wide inter-state variation (R) is the cause of the 'may' language (A), reversing the actual causal direction.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Wide variation in Gram Sabha powers across Indian states is a documented reality — Kerala has strong formal powers, while many states have minimal statutory empowerment. A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Article 243A's use of 'may' rather than 'shall' is a factual constitutional provision — it gives state legislatures complete discretion on whether to empower Gram Sabha. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? Yes — R directly and causally explains A. The wide inter-state variation (A) is the direct consequence of the permissive 'may' language in Article 243A (R). States that chose to empower Gram Sabha extensively (like Kerala) and states that chose not to — both exercised the discretion that 'may' provides. R is the causal explanation for A.
Both A and R are correct AND R causally explains A — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the reversed-causation design — students often confuse the direction of causation when both A and R are correct. The wide inter-state variation (A) is the effect; the 'may' language in Article 243A (R) is the cause. Students who are confused about direction may select option (b) thinking the causal link is absent. In this case, the causal link is genuine and direct — making option (a) correct, which itself is a trap for students trained to be suspicious of option (a) in assertion-reason questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243A's permissive 'may' language is the constitutional root cause of asymmetric Gram Sabha empowerment across India.

Assertion (A): There is wide documented variation in Gram Sabha's actual powers across Indian states — from Kerala's model where Gram Sabha formally approves Panchayat plans, to states where Gram Sabha is little more than a symbolic gathering. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): Article 243A uses the word 'may' — 'The Legislature of a State may, by law, endow the Gram Sabha with such powers and functions.' This is the precise constitutional text, and it is factually correct.

Causal link: R directly and causally explains A. The wide inter-state variation exists because the Constitution does not mandate any minimum empowerment — states exercise the discretion that 'may' gives them in vastly different ways. Kerala chose maximum empowerment; many states chose minimal empowerment — both outcomes are constitutionally permitted under 'may'.

Value Addition:
• The 'may' vs. 'shall' distinction appears in both Article 243A (Gram Sabha powers) and Article 243G (Panchayat planning functions) — both create structural gaps.
• Reform proposals consistently advocate amending 'may' to 'shall' in Article 243A as the single most important constitutional change for Gram Sabha empowerment.
• This asymmetry is described as the 'missing link' in India's decentralisation architecture.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 243D reservation applies to Gram Panchayat seats not Gram Sabha
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly associates 243D with women's reservation but then incorrectly extends its application to 'all tiers of Panchayat and Gram Sabha membership', exploiting students' tendency to over-generalise the reservation provision.
elimination_logic: The blank must complete a factually accurate statement about Article 243D's scope of application.
Article 243D mandates not less than 1/3 reservation for women in offices of Chairpersons and in seats in Panchayats at each tier.
Eliminate (a): 243D applies to Panchayat elected seats, not to Gram Sabha membership — Gram Sabha has no reserved seats as all voters are members.
Eliminate (b): 'All tiers of Panchayat and Gram Sabha membership' over-extends the provision — Gram Sabha has no seats to reserve.
Eliminate (c): 243D applies to all three tiers of Panchayats — village, intermediate, and district — not just the district tier.
Confirm (d): Article 243D applies to elected seats in Panchayat bodies (all three tiers) — not to Gram Sabha, whose membership is the entire electorate.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Gram Sabha for Gram Panchayat in the application of Article 243D. Students who know that 243D mandates women's reservation in Panchayati Raj institutions often extend this to Gram Sabha without recognising that Gram Sabha has no 'seats' — it is constituted from the entire electorate. Option (b) is carefully crafted to include 'all tiers' (partially true) while adding 'and Gram Sabha membership' (false) — a classic partial-truth disguised as a scope extension.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 243D is the constitutional provision for women's reservation in Panchayati Raj, and its precise scope is a frequent UPSC test point.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 243D does apply to women's reservation but NOT to Gram Sabha membership — the provision covers elected seats in Panchayat bodies only.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'All tiers of Panchayat' is correct but 'and Gram Sabha membership' is false — Gram Sabha has no reserved seats as it is constituted from the entire electorate automatically.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 243D applies to all three tiers (village, intermediate, district) — restricting it to only the district (Zila Parishad) tier is factually wrong.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 243D mandates not less than one-third reservation for women in elected seats and offices of Chairpersons in Panchayats at all three tiers — village, intermediate, and district. Gram Sabha is excluded because it has no elected seats.

Value Addition:
• Reservation under 243D is to be allocated by rotation to different constituencies in each Panchayat.
• Over 17 states have extended women's reservation to 50% through state legislation.
• The total number of women elected to Panchayati Raj institutions exceeds 1.4 million — the world's largest experiment in reserved political representation.

solution.concept_anchor: FRA Gram Sabha at hamlet level not revenue village level
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students know that PESA applies to Fifth Schedule areas and might assume that the FRA, also dealing with forest communities in tribal areas, similarly uses the revenue village as its base unit for Gram Sabha.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): FRA's operative Gram Sabha is at the hamlet/habitation level — not the revenue village. This pair is incorrectly matched.

Eliminate (b): Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC) is the APPELLATE body above Gram Sabha under FRA — not a body that receives claims directly before Gram Sabha. The description misrepresents the SDLC's role in the hierarchy.
Eliminate (d): PESA applies to Fifth Schedule areas of 10 specific states — Assam is a Sixth Schedule state and is NOT covered by PESA. This pair is incorrectly matched.
Confirm (c): PESA does empower Gram Sabha in Fifth Schedule areas to regulate money-lending — this is an authentic and correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a)'s conflation trap merges the FRA Gram Sabha with the standard revenue village Gram Sabha. FRA specifically recognises that forest-dwelling communities are often organised at hamlet/habitation level — smaller than revenue villages — and designates the Gram Sabha at that level as the competent authority. Students who know FRA involves Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas may assume it uses the same revenue village unit as PESA and Part IX generally, making option (a) appear correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Correctly pairing statutory provisions with their precise institutional descriptions requires knowing the exact level at which each law operates.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: FRA's operative Gram Sabha is at the hamlet or habitation level, not the revenue village level. Forest-dwelling communities may be too small to form a revenue village Gram Sabha — FRA accommodates this by working at the habitation level.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: The Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC) under FRA is the first appellate authority above the Gram Sabha — not a body that receives initial claims. Claims are first processed by Gram Sabha before being forwarded upward.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: PESA specifically empowers Gram Sabha in Fifth Schedule areas to regulate and control money-lending to prevent exploitation of tribal communities — an authentic PESA provision.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: PESA applies to 10 Fifth Schedule states — Assam is governed by the Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils) and is NOT a PESA state.

Value Addition:
• The 10 PESA states: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan.
• Under FRA, claims proceed: Gram Sabha → SDLC → District Level Committee (DLC).
• FRA's three-tier claims hierarchy is a frequently tested structure in UPSC questions on tribal rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Gram Panchayat executive dominance over Gram Sabha in practice

statement_analysis.statement: Elite capture of Gram Sabha refers to the phenomenon where dominant caste or economic groups control the agenda and outcomes of Gram Sabha meetings, effectively defeating its constitutional purpose as an instrument of inclusive direct democracy.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the documented phenomenon of elite capture — a primary structural challenge noted by the Second ARC and academic studies — where powerful village groups monopolise Gram Sabha deliberations, undermining representation of marginalised communities.

statement_analysis.statement: In practice, the Gram Panchayat (the executive body) rarely dominates the Gram Sabha (the deliberative body) because Article 243A grants Gram Sabha explicit powers to override Gram Panchayat decisions — establishing a clear constitutional hierarchy.
statement_analysis.reason: In practice, the reverse is true — the Gram Panchayat often dominates the Gram Sabha because it controls administrative resources, information, and implementation. Moreover, Article 243A does NOT grant Gram Sabha explicit powers to override Gram Panchayat decisions — such powers, where they exist, come from state legislation.

statement_analysis.statement: The introduction of E-Gram Sabha platforms and mandatory video recording of meetings has fully resolved the problem of proxy attendance and meeting capture in most Indian states.
statement_analysis.reason: While E-Gram Sabha and video recording are remedial measures, they have NOT fully resolved problems of proxy attendance and meeting capture. Digital divides, implementation gaps, and the structural factors that cause elite capture persist — these measures have had limited effectiveness, especially in remote areas.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 accurately describes elite capture, and students may mark it as 'NOT correct' if they misread the question stem, selecting '1 only' instead of correctly identifying Statements 2 and 3 as the incorrect ones.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Accurate description of elite capture phenomenon as documented by Second ARC and academic research. Statement 1 IS correct — it does NOT belong in the answer to 'which is NOT correct'.

Evaluate Statement 2: Claims that Gram Panchayat 'rarely dominates' Gram Sabha AND that Article 243A gives Gram Sabha override powers — both are factually wrong. In reality, Gram Panchayat dominance is the norm in practice. Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: Claims E-Gram Sabha has 'fully resolved' proxy attendance — this is an absolute claim that does not reflect reality; digital divide and structural factors persist. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 employs reversed-causation: students know that constitutionally Gram Sabha is supposed to be the principal and Gram Panchayat the agent, so they may assume this constitutional design is reflected in practice. The reality is the opposite — Gram Panchayat executive dominance over Gram Sabha is a well-documented dysfunction. Statement 3 uses an absolute qualifier ('fully resolved') that makes it factually incorrect — a classic scope-extension trap layered within a reversed-causation question.
solution.final_explanation:
Gram Sabha's structural challenges are as important for UPSC as its formal powers — understanding the gap between constitutional design and functional reality is tested directly.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Elite capture is the documented phenomenon where dominant groups monopolise Gram Sabha outcomes — a primary finding of the Second ARC on local governance.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The claim has two false elements: (i) In practice, Gram Panchayat executive dominance over Gram Sabha is the norm — Gram Panchayat controls information, funds, and administrative machinery; (ii) Article 243A does NOT grant Gram Sabha powers to override Gram Panchayat decisions — such powers, where they exist, are state legislation creations.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The absolute claim that E-Gram Sabha has 'fully resolved' proxy attendance and meeting capture is false. Digital divide, infrastructure gaps, and social power structures that enable capture persist, limiting effectiveness.

Value Addition:
• Proxy attendance refers to Gram Sabha meetings conducted with fabricated attendance records — a documented malpractice.
• Bihar's mandatory video recording of Gram Sabha meetings is a pioneering state-level reform.
• The Second ARC recommended incentivising attendance and ensuring administrative support for Gram Sabha meetings as systemic solutions.

solution.concept_anchor: MGNREGA 2005, PMAY-G 2016, FRA 2006 — timeline of Gram Sabha statutory roles
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know MGNREGA preceded FRA may correctly sequence those two but might misplace PMAY-G, which was launched in 2016 (well after both), placing it between them instead of last.
elimination_logic: Anchor Event 1: MGNREGA was enacted in 2005 (came into force 2006 in phases) — first major CSS to give Gram Sabha a statutory social audit role. This must be first or second.
Anchor Event 2: FRA was enacted in December 2006 — after MGNREGA's enactment in 2005. Gram Sabha's quasi-judicial claim verification role under FRA came with this Act.

Anchor Event 3: PMAY-G (Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana Gramin) was launched in November 2016 — significantly later than both MGNREGA and FRA. Gram Sabha's Awaas+ list preparation role came with this scheme.
Correct chronological sequence: MGNREGA (2005) → FRA (2006) → PMAY-G (2016) — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets students who know MGNREGA and FRA are both from the mid-2000s but are uncertain about the exact sequence (MGNREGA 2005, FRA 2006). Some may reverse these two, placing FRA before MGNREGA. The subtler trap is for students who place PMAY-G between MGNREGA and FRA, not knowing its 2016 launch date. The question tests knowledge of all three dates simultaneously.
solution.final_explanation:
These three pieces of legislation represent successive expansions of Gram Sabha's statutory roles in welfare governance.

• MGNREGA (2005): The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was enacted in 2005 and progressively rolled out from 2006. Section 17 established the statutory social audit mandate for Gram Sabha — the first time any legislation made Gram Sabha's audit role a statutory obligation. This must come first in the sequence.
• FRA (2006): The Forest Rights Act was enacted in December 2006 — after MGNREGA. FRA designated Gram Sabha as the competent authority for verifying and processing forest rights claims, giving it a unique quasi-judicial role. This comes second.
• PMAY-G (2016): Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana Gramin was launched in November 2016 — a decade after FRA. Under PMAY-G, Gram Sabha prepares the Awaas+ beneficiary list using SECC data as a mandatory step. This comes last.

Wrong options all misplace at least one of these events, with options reversing MGNREGA and FRA being the most dangerous.

Value Addition:
• MGNREGA came into force in 200 districts on February 2, 2006 — often confused with its 2005 enactment date.
• FRA was preceded by a prolonged political struggle over tribal forest rights dating back to the 1980s.
• PMAY-G replaced the earlier Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) — launched on November 20, 2016.

solution.concept_anchor: PESA Gram Sabha powers over tribal land alienation in Fifth Schedule areas
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know FRA is associated with forest communities and tribal land may apply FRA instead of PESA, not knowing that PESA's specific provision on preventing and restoring tribal land alienation is the more directly applicable provision in this scenario.
elimination_logic: Identify key scenario elements: (1) Scheduled Area (Fifth Schedule state), (2) tribal land being alienated to non-tribal persons, (3) Gram Sabha passing a resolution to prevent the transfer and restore already transferred land.

Eliminate (a): FRA's Gram Sabha role relates to forest rights claims verification — not to preventing alienation of agricultural/habitation land to non-tribal persons. FRA is about forest dwellers' rights to land they traditionally cultivated, not general tribal land protection.
Eliminate (c): Gram Nyayalayas Act (2008) establishes separate judicial courts at block level — Gram Sabha has no role under this Act.
Eliminate (d): The scenario is about land alienation prevention and restoration — this is a specific PESA power, more directly applicable than FRA's community forest rights framework.

Confirm (b): PESA specifically empowers Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas to prevent alienation of tribal land to non-tribal persons and to restore unlawfully transferred land — the scenario precisely describes this PESA power.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap here is the common confusion between PESA and FRA in tribal land contexts. FRA deals with rights over forest land; PESA's land protection provisions deal with the broader protection of tribal land (including agricultural and habitation land) from alienation to non-tribal persons. A student who correctly identifies the Scheduled Area context but applies FRA (associated with 'tribal land and forests') instead of PESA (which has the specific anti-alienation provision) will select option (d).
solution.final_explanation:
PESA and FRA address different dimensions of tribal land rights, and identifying which law applies requires knowing each law's specific provisions.

Scenario analysis: The scenario describes (1) a Fifth Schedule area, (2) tribal land being transferred to non-tribal persons, and (3) a Gram Sabha resolution to prevent further transfers and restore already transferred land. This maps directly onto PESA's anti-alienation provision.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: FRA's Gram Sabha role is in verifying claims for forest rights — it addresses rights of forest dwellers to land they traditionally cultivated in forest areas. It does not specifically address prevention of tribal land alienation to non-tribal persons in the manner PESA does.
• Option (b) — Correct: PESA explicitly empowers Gram Sabha to prevent alienation of tribal land to non-tribal persons and to restore land that has been unlawfully transferred — the scenario is a textbook application of this PESA provision.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Gram Nyayalayas Act creates separate judicial bodies at the block level; Gram Sabha has no role under that Act.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Indian Forest Act governs state forest administration — Gram Sabha has no authority under it.

Value Addition:
• The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act and PESA are complementary but address different land categories.
• PESA also empowers Gram Sabha to restore possession of land from which tribal persons have been displaced.
• Supreme Court rulings have held that state laws permitting tribal land alienation must conform to PESA in Scheduled Areas.

solution.concept_anchor: Ashok Mehta Committee recommended two-tier structure reducing Gram Sabha emphasis
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know L.M. Singhvi Committee recommended constitutional status for Panchayats may also assume it recommended a specific number of minimum powers for Gram Sabha — the 'nucleus' description is correct but the 'minimum mandatory powers' detail is fabricated.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj structure — not specifically calling Gram Sabha the 'primary unit of self-governance' in these words, and it did not specifically recommend constitutional protection for Gram Sabha.

Eliminate (b): L.M. Singhvi Committee described Gram Sabha as the 'nucleus' of decentralisation and recommended constitutional status for Panchayats — but specifying 'minimum ten mandatory powers' is a fabricated detail not associated with Singhvi Committee.

Eliminate (d): Gram Sabha under Article 243(b) consists of ALL registered voters — not specifically elected or nominated members. Describing it as composed of 'elected and nominated members' is factually wrong.

Confirm (c): Ashok Mehta Committee (1978) did recommend a two-tier Panchayati Raj structure (Mandal and Zila), which would have reduced the three-tier system — and implicitly diminished the role of the village-level body (Gram Sabha). This is a correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in option (b) pairs the L.M. Singhvi Committee (correctly) with an additional fabricated detail about 'minimum ten mandatory powers for Gram Sabha'. Students who know Singhvi Committee is associated with Gram Sabha's 'nucleus' description and constitutional status recommendation may not notice the fabricated '10 minimum mandatory powers' detail — selecting (b) without realising it contains a plausible-fabrication element. Option (c) about Ashok Mehta is correctly matched and tests precise knowledge of his committee's two-tier recommendation.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing between the three major Panchayati Raj committees' recommendations on Gram Sabha's role requires precise knowledge of each committee's specific positions.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier structure (village, block, district). While it supported Gram Panchayat, it did not specifically describe Gram Sabha in the terms stated, and its primary recommendation was structural, not specifically about Gram Sabha empowerment.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) described Gram Sabha as the 'nucleus' of decentralisation and recommended constitutional status for Panchayats — but 'minimum ten mandatory powers' is a fabricated detail not associated with this committee.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Ashok Mehta Committee (1978) recommended compressing Panchayati Raj to two tiers — a Mandal Panchayat at the sub-block level and a Zila Parishad at the district level. This structural recommendation would have eliminated the village-tier and diminished Gram Sabha's institutional role.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Gram Sabha under Article 243(b) consists of all persons registered as voters in the village's electoral rolls — not elected or nominated members. Members are automatically all adult voters, not elected.

Value Addition:
• Ashok Mehta Committee's report was accepted in principle but largely unimplemented before the 73rd Amendment superseded it.
• The Singhvi Committee report was the most influential in leading to the 73rd Amendment.
• Balwant Rai Mehta's three tiers remain the basis of Panchayati Raj today.

solution.concept_anchor: PESA Fifth Schedule vs. Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils

statement_analysis.statement: Sixth Schedule areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram are governed by Autonomous District Councils — Part IX of the Constitution (which defines Gram Sabha) does not apply to these areas.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils for tribal areas in these four northeastern states. The 73rd Amendment's Part IX provisions, including the constitutional definition of Gram Sabha, were not extended to Sixth Schedule areas — these operate under a separate constitutional framework.

statement_analysis.statement: Traditional village institutions like Dorbar Shnong in Meghalaya perform functions similar to those of a Gram Sabha, and they are constitutionally recognised as Gram Sabhas under Part IX because they satisfy the functional requirements of Article 243(b).
statement_analysis.reason: Dorbar Shnong and similar traditional institutions are NOT constitutional Gram Sabhas under Part IX. They are traditional/customary institutions recognised under Sixth Schedule arrangements — functioning like Gram Sabhas in practice but having no legal identity under Article 243(b) of the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: A state legislature can exempt any hilly or tribal area from the applicability of Part IX under Article 243M, and this exemption power has been used to exclude certain areas from the Gram Sabha framework.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 243M explicitly allows for exemption of certain areas (Scheduled Areas, tribal areas, hill districts like those in Darjeeling) from Part IX's provisions — and this power has been exercised in various states to limit Gram Sabha's applicability.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only Statement 1' is a strong distractor because students who are uncertain about Statement 3's Article 243M exemption provision may be unsure whether to include it, defaulting to only the clearly verifiable Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Sixth Schedule governs Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram through Autonomous District Councils — Part IX including Gram Sabha definition does not apply. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Dorbar Shnong is a traditional institution, not a constitutional Gram Sabha under Article 243(b) — Part IX does not apply in Meghalaya (Sixth Schedule state). The claim of constitutional recognition is wrong. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 243M explicitly provides for exemptions from Part IX for certain areas — this provision is real and has been used. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the functional similarity between traditional institutions like Dorbar Shnong and constitutional Gram Sabha. Students who know that these traditional bodies perform Gram Sabha-like functions may assume they have been constitutionally recognised as Gram Sabhas — especially if they know the 73rd Amendment accommodated traditional governance in some contexts. In reality, Sixth Schedule areas operate entirely outside Part IX — traditional institutions there have no legal identity as Article 243(b) Gram Sabhas.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional architecture for tribal governance in India has two distinct and non-overlapping frameworks — Part IX (including Gram Sabha) and the Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils).

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils for Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram — complete constitutional frameworks in their own right. Part IX (Panchayati Raj including Gram Sabha) simply does not apply in these areas.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Dorbar Shnong (Meghalaya) is a traditional Khasi village institution that performs community governance functions. It operates under customary law and Sixth Schedule arrangements — it has no constitutional identity as a Gram Sabha under Article 243(b). Functional similarity does not create constitutional equivalence.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 243M(2) empowers the President/Governor to exempt Scheduled Areas, tribal areas, and specified hill districts from all or part of Part IX. This provision has been used in Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram, Meghalaya, and hill districts of West Bengal (Darjeeling).

Value Addition:
• Article 243M also exempts the states of Nagaland and Meghalaya from Part IX entirely.
• The Sixth Schedule areas have the President's power to annex or re-define autonomous districts.
• Manipur's hill tribal areas are governed by district councils under the Manipur (Hill Areas) District Councils Act — separate from Part IX.

solution.concept_anchor: e-GramSwaraj and Svamitva — correct institutional roles

statement_analysis.statement: The Svamitva Scheme mandates that a Gram Sabha ODF (Open Defecation Free) declaration is the precondition for initiating drone-based property mapping in any village.
statement_analysis.reason: The ODF declaration by Gram Sabha is a step under Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin), not a precondition for Svamitva Scheme's drone mapping. Svamitva's property mapping is a separate exercise under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj — it has no ODF prerequisite.

statement_analysis.statement: Kerala's People's Planning Campaign devolved approximately 35–40% of state plan resources to Gram Panchayats with Gram Sabha as the mandatory oversight body — making it the strongest model of Gram Sabha empowerment in India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Kerala People's Planning Campaign (1996) did devolve around 35–40% of state plan funds to Panchayats, with Gram Sabha playing a formal mandatory role in approving development plans — this is widely considered the strongest implementation of Gram Sabha empowerment in India.

statement_analysis.statement: The e-GramSwaraj portal, by integrating Gram Panchayat planning and accounting functions, functions as a substitute for Gram Sabha meetings — enabling online voting and resolution-passing by registered voters without requiring physical assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: e-GramSwaraj is a transparency and accountability tool for Gram Panchayat — it makes plans and expenditure accessible for Gram Sabha review but does NOT substitute for physical Gram Sabha meetings. Online voting and resolution-passing are not features of e-GramSwaraj.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 3 as wrong (e-GramSwaraj does not enable online voting) may overlook the fabricated linkage in Statement 1 between Svamitva and ODF declaration, thinking the ODF-Gram Sabha connection they know from SBM-G also applies to Svamitva.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Svamitva's drone mapping has no precondition of Gram Sabha ODF declaration — ODF declaration is an SBM-G requirement, not a Svamitva requirement. Conflating two separate schemes. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Kerala's People's Planning Campaign did devolve 35–40% of state plan funds with Gram Sabha as mandatory oversight — this is a factually accurate and well-documented claim. Statement 2 IS correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: e-GramSwaraj is a transparency portal — it does not substitute Gram Sabha meetings or enable online resolution-passing by registered voters. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses plausible-fabrication: students know that Gram Sabha is associated with ODF declarations under SBM-G, and they know Svamitva involves Gram Sabha in dispute resolution. Linking the two in a 'precondition' relationship sounds plausible because it combines two genuine Gram Sabha functions. But the specific claim — that ODF declaration is a precondition for Svamitva mapping — is fabricated. Statement 3 is a scope-extension: e-GramSwaraj improves transparency but does not replace physical deliberation.
solution.final_explanation:
Digital initiatives related to Gram Sabha must be understood with precision — each has a specific and limited functional scope.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Svamitva Scheme (drone mapping for property cards) and SBM-G (ODF declaration) are separate schemes with separate processes. Gram Sabha's ODF resolution is required under SBM-G, not as a precondition for Svamitva. Conflating the two schemes' Gram Sabha requirements is a fabricated connection.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Kerala's 1996 People's Planning Campaign is the gold standard for Gram Sabha empowerment — devolving 35–40% of state plan resources with mandatory Gram Sabha approval for Panchayat development plans.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: e-GramSwaraj integrates Gram Panchayat planning and accounting into a digital platform — it is a transparency tool that enables Gram Sabha members to access information, but it does not and cannot substitute for physical Gram Sabha meetings or enable online resolution-passing.

Value Addition:
• Svamitva aimed to cover 6.62 lakh villages across India with drone-based property mapping.
• Kerala's People's Planning Campaign is studied internationally as a model of participatory budgeting at the local level.
• e-GramSwaraj is linked to the audit systems of CAG — enabling cross-verification of Gram Panchayat expenditure.
